text: said it supports the request and can accommodate it and that its Trees and Sidewalks Program repairs severe sidewalk damage from tree roots at owner occupied 1 to 3 family homes. It also said more funding would help but it can't expand at current staffing
source: Agency supports and can accommodate. NYC Parks' Trees & Sidewalks Program can help repair severe sidewalk damage caused by tree root growth in front of one-, two-, or three-family properties that are owner-occupied and used exclusively for residential purposes (NYC Tax Class 1). Funding for this program is limited, and repairs are made based on a rating system that includes the severity of damage, amount of pedestrian traffic, and the size and condition of the tree. If you are a homeowner with time-sensitive needs for sidewalk repair, or you own a non-Tax Class 1 property that is not eligible for Parks’ Trees & Sidewalks Program, repairing the sidewalk through an independent contractor is often the quickest solution. Anyone performing work on or within 50 feet of a City tree must obtain a Tree Work Permit from Parks before beginning work. If you wish to file a claim against the City of New York for the cost of repairs you performed to your sidewalk because of damage that you believe was caused by a City tree, you may do so by filing a claim with the New York City Comptroller’s Office within 90 days of performing the repair. Due to limited resources, the Trees & Sidewalks Program is only able to repair the most severely damaged sites across all five boroughs. We agree that additional funding would increase the capacity of this program, but additional funding cannot be accommodated with current staffing levels.

source: This request has already been completed. HPD employs a variety of strategies to conduct outreach and distribute critical information to tenants and property owners across the city. These efforts include tabling events, the HPD Van, and participation in resource fairs, often in collaboration with local community-based organizations, community boards, and elected officials. For homeowners, HPD offers two key initiatives—the Homeowner Help Desk and HomeFix—both administered by the Center for New York City Neighborhoods. For tenants, HPD has expanded its Partners in Preservation program, which offers substantial funding to community-based organizations to strengthen their organizing teams and extend services and resources to more tenants in need. text: said it supports the request but can't accommodate it and that funding for its block pruning program was restored after the pandemic and its 7-year pruning cycle matches industry standards. It also said it agrees more funding is needed to add staff, but that funding can't be determined yet
source: Agency supports but cannot accommodate. Funding for our block pruning program was restored following the pandemic, and our 7-year street tree pruning cycle matches industry standards. If individual trees need pruning for public safety, we encourage anyone to submit a service request by locating the tree on the NYC Tree Map (and clicking on the “report a problem” tab), calling 311, or using our online tree service request system. Our inspectors will visit the tree and determine the appropriate action in accordance with our Tree Risk Management program. More details can be found on the Parks website: https://www.nycgovparks.org/services/forestry/risk-management. NYC Parks' Climber & Pruner Training Program is an in-house training program that connects current entry-level Parks employees with the training to become Climber & Pruners. With this program, Parks expects to add 15-20 new Climber & Pruners to the workforce every 15 months to help mitigate recruitment and hiring challenges. We agree with the need for more funding to increase staff, but that funding cannot be determined at this time.

text: said it supports the request and can accommodate it and that it will work with us to study protected crosstown bike lanes in Midtown Manhattan, and that it scheduled conventional bike lanes on West 18th and West 22nd Streets, extending the existing lanes, for its FY2026 resurfacing season
source: Agency supports and can accommodate. The New York City Department of Transportation (DOT) is dedicated to enhancing the safety and efficiency of the city’s streets. They will collaborate with Community Board 4 to introduce bicycle facilities in the area. The DOT will investigate the possibility of creating protected crosstown bicycle lanes in Midtown Manhattan. As you may know, designing this type of facility in the area presents challenges, including high vehicle volumes, curbside access requirements, and the need for network connectivity. The agency will continue to assess the feasibility of these improvements as it works to expand and upgrade the bicycle network. Additionally, the agency will install conventional bike lanes on West 18th and West 22nd Streets by extending the two existing bike lanes. This work is scheduled to be done during our resurfacing season in FY2026.
